title: Parasites: how lice, ticks, worms and mosquitoes live on other living beings

summary.text: A head louse spends their whole life on a human head, holding on to hairs and drinking a little blood. A living being who lives on or inside another living being, and feeds from them, is called a parasite. The one they live on is the host. Lice, fleas and ticks live on the outside of the body. Some worms live inside the gut. The malaria parasite lives part of their life in a mosquito and part in a person. Each parasite reaches us by one path, so we stay safe by closing that path: a fine comb, chappals, clean hands, a mosquito net.
summary.art: A child's head seen close up, with a tiny louse holding a hair, and around it small drawings of a flea, a tick, a worm and a mosquito, each joined to the child by a dotted line.

intro.hook: Hold a khus khus seed on your fingertip. A head louse's egg is smaller than this seed, and is glued to one hair. Your comb at home has gaps much wider than that. So how can anyone comb the eggs out?
intro.text: In this unit you meet the parasites that live on people: head lice, fleas, ticks and worms. You find out what problem each one has, and how their body solves it. You test which comb can catch something as small as a louse egg. You follow the malaria parasite from a person into a mosquito and back. And you learn the simple habits that keep every one of them off you.
intro.art: A child's fingertip holding a single khus khus seed, next to a fine-tooth comb and an ordinary comb lying side by side on a table.

outcomes: I can say what a parasite and a host are, and give examples.
I can explain how a head louse holds on to hair, and why a fine-tooth comb removes lice and their eggs.
I can describe how fleas and ticks reach a host, and how to keep them off.
I can say how worms get into the body, and how chappals, clean hands and washed food stop them.
I can explain how a mosquito carries malaria from one person to another, and how nets, covers and fans keep us safe.
I can tell how Ronald Ross showed that malaria comes from a parasite carried by a mosquito, not from bad air.

terms.meaning: A living being who lives on or inside another living being, and takes food from them.
terms.example: A head louse is a parasite. They live in your hair and drink a little of your blood.
terms.art: A tiny louse holding a hair on a child's head.

terms.meaning: The living being a parasite lives on or in.
terms.example: When a dog has fleas, the dog is the fleas' host.
terms.art: A street dog scratching behind one ear, with two small fleas drawn in a circle beside the ear.

terms.meaning: A tiny insect with no wings who lives in hair and drinks blood. A head louse is about as big as a sesame seed.
terms.example: Head lice spread when two heads touch, for example when friends lean together over one phone.
terms.art: A head louse drawn large, with six legs, each ending in a curved claw around a hair.

terms.meaning: A louse's egg, or the empty egg case left after the young louse hatches. The mother glues each egg to one hair, close to the scalp.
terms.example: Nits look like tiny white or brown dots stuck to hairs. They do not shake off like dandruff.
terms.art: One hair with a small oval egg glued to it near the root, next to a loose flake of dandruff.

terms.meaning: A tiny insect with no wings who jumps very far and drinks the blood of animals such as cats, dogs and rats.
terms.example: A cat flea can jump about 20 cm, about a hundred times their own length.
terms.art: A flea mid-jump in a high arc over a ruler, with a cat's tail at one side.

terms.meaning: A small animal with eight legs, a cousin of spiders, who holds on to skin and drinks blood for several days.
terms.example: Brown dog ticks are common on dogs in Indian cities. They swell up as they feed.
terms.art: A flat brown tick next to the same tick swollen like a bean after feeding.

terms.meaning: A small fly with long legs. The female drinks blood to make her eggs. Some mosquitoes carry the parasites and viruses that cause malaria and dengue.
terms.example: A mosquito sits on your arm at dusk, and the bite itches afterwards.
terms.art: A female mosquito standing on an arm, her long mouthpart touching the skin.

terms.meaning: The long, thin mouthpart of a mosquito. Inside its cover are six fine needles.
terms.example: A mosquito pushes her proboscis into your skin to find a tiny blood vessel.
terms.art: A mosquito's head drawn large, with the cover of the proboscis bent back and six fine needles going into skin.

terms.meaning: An illness that brings fever and shivering. A tiny one-celled parasite causes it, and some mosquitoes carry that parasite.
terms.example: A person with malaria may shiver under a blanket, then feel very hot, then sweat. A doctor's blood test shows the parasite.
terms.art: A child resting under a blanket while a health worker looks at a drop of blood through a microscope.

terms.meaning: The name scientists give the malaria parasite. Each one is a single cell, far too small to see without a microscope.
terms.example: Plasmodium lives in a person's liver and then inside their red blood cells.
terms.art: A round red blood cell drawn large, with a tiny ring-shaped parasite inside.

terms.meaning: A living being who carries a germ or parasite from one host to another. The vector is usually not the one who makes you ill.
terms.example: The Anopheles mosquito is the vector of malaria. The parasite inside her is what causes the illness.
terms.art: A mosquito drawn as a small boat, carrying a tiny parasite from one sleeping person to another.

terms.meaning: A worm who can live in a person's gut. Their eggs are passed in poo and can get into soil.
terms.example: Roundworm eggs can get into the mouth from unwashed hands or unwashed vegetables grown in soil.
terms.art: Two hands washing a carrot under a tap, with a magnified drop showing tiny eggs being washed away.

terms.meaning: A small worm whose young live in soil and get in through the skin of bare feet. In the gut, the worm holds on and drinks blood.
terms.example: Wearing chappals on soil keeps hookworms out.
terms.art: A bare foot on muddy soil next to the same foot in a chappal, with a cross over the bare foot.

terms.meaning: Taking a medicine that clears worms out of the gut.
terms.example: On National Deworming Day, schools and anganwadis in India give children a worm medicine called albendazole.
terms.art: A teacher giving a tablet and a glass of water to a line of children in school uniform.

explanations.context: This card says what a parasite is, and what a host is.
explanations.definition: A parasite is a living being who lives on or inside another living being, the host, and takes food from them. The host is usually harmed a little, but most parasites do not kill their host.
explanations.description: Some parasites live on the outside of the body. Head lice, fleas and ticks hold on to hair or skin and drink blood. Others live inside. Roundworms and hookworms live in the gut, and the malaria parasite lives in the liver and the blood. Plants can be parasites too. Dodder is a yellow climbing plant with no green leaves. Dodder winds round another plant and pushes tiny suckers into their stem to take food. Birds can be parasites in another way. The koel lays her eggs in a crow's nest, and the crows raise the koel chicks as their own.
examples: A head louse lives in human hair and drinks blood several times a day.
Dodder twines round a plant on a roadside fence and feeds from their stem.
A koel chick grows up in a crow's nest, fed by the crow parents.
explanations.art: Three small pictures: a louse on a hair, yellow dodder threads wrapped round a green plant, and a crow feeding a dark koel chick in a nest.

explanations.concept: Head lice: how a louse holds on
explanations.context: This card is about head lice: the problem a louse has, and how their body solves it.
explanations.definition: A head louse is a small insect with no wings, up to 3 mm long. Head lice live only on people's heads, and drink blood from the scalp.
explanations.description: A louse has one big problem: staying on. A head moves, gets washed and gets combed. A louse cannot fly or jump, and if they fall off, they usually die within a day or two. So each of their six legs ends in a curved claw that closes round a single hair, the way your fingers close round a rope. A mother louse also solves a problem for her eggs. Eggs need warmth to hatch. So she glues each egg to a hair right next to the warm scalp. The glue is so strong that shampoo and water do not loosen it. The egg hatches in about 8 days. The young louse grows into an adult in about 9 more days, and a female can then lay up to 6 eggs a day.
examples: Lice spread when heads touch, for example in a group photo or when friends lean over one book.
Lice live on clean hair just as well as on unwashed hair. Getting lice says nothing about how clean someone is.
Dogs and cats do not carry human head lice.
explanations.art: A louse drawn large, holding a hair with curved claws, and an egg glued to the same hair close to the scalp.

explanations.concept: Getting lice out: the fine-tooth comb
explanations.context: This card is about how families get rid of head lice, and why a fine-tooth comb works.
explanations.definition: A fine-tooth lice comb has teeth so close together that a louse or a louse egg cannot slip between them. Combing wet hair from the roots to the ends pulls lice and eggs out.
explanations.description: In Tamil Nadu this comb is often called an eer kolli, the nit remover. The gaps between its teeth are much narrower than an ordinary comb's. Families wet the hair and add conditioner or a little coconut oil, so the comb slides and the lice move slowly. Then they comb every part of the head from the scalp outwards, and wipe the comb on a white tissue to see what came out. One combing misses a few eggs. So the NHS, the health service in the United Kingdom, says to comb on days 1, 5, 9 and 13. That catches young lice as they hatch, before they are old enough to lay eggs. A doctor or chemist can also give a lotion that kills lice. A grown-up uses it, following the instructions exactly.
examples: A 3,700-year-old ivory comb found at Lachish, in Israel, has a line carved on it asking the comb to root out the lice of the hair and the beard.
Wiping the comb on a white tissue shows each louse clearly.
explanations.art: A grandmother combing a girl's wet hair on a doorstep in morning light, wiping a fine comb on a white cloth.

explanations.concept: Fleas: how a tiny jumper finds a big host
explanations.context: This card is about fleas, who live on cats, dogs and rats, and sometimes bite people.
explanations.definition: A flea is a small insect with no wings, about 2 to 3 mm long, who drinks the blood of mammals and birds.
explanations.description: A flea's problem is getting on to a host who is huge and keeps moving. Their answer is a jump. A pad in each back leg is made of a springy material called resilin. The flea squeezes the pad, holds it, and lets go all at once, like a catapult. A cat flea can jump about 20 cm, about a hundred times their own length. Once on the animal, a flea's body is flat from side to side, so they slide between hairs. Spines on their body point backwards, so they are hard to pull out. Flea eggs fall off into the animal's bed. So washing a pet's bedding and vacuuming the floor remove the eggs.
examples: A street dog scratching hard behind the ears may have fleas.
Fleas on rats once spread plague. In 1898 Paul-Louis Simond, working in Karachi and Bombay, found that rat fleas carry the plague germ.
explanations.art: A flea drawn large from the side, flat like a seed, with back legs folded ready to jump and backward spines along the body.

explanations.concept: Ticks: wait, climb on and hold on
explanations.context: This card is about ticks: how they find a host and how to take one off safely.
explanations.definition: A tick is a small arachnid, a cousin of spiders. An adult tick has eight legs. Ticks hold on to the skin and drink blood, often for several days.
explanations.description: A tick cannot jump or fly, so they wait. They climb a blade of grass and hold out their front legs. Those front legs have sense organs that detect the breath, warmth and smell of an animal walking past. When a dog or a person brushes by, the tick grabs on. Then they cut into the skin and push in a mouthpart covered with backward-pointing barbs, like a fish hook. Many ticks also make a kind of glue to fix themselves in place. That is why you must not tug a tick or squeeze their body. A grown-up takes hold of the tick with fine tweezers right next to the skin and pulls straight up, slowly and steadily. Then they wash the bite with soap and water.
examples: Brown dog ticks are common on dogs in Indian cities, inside homes and kennels.
In 1957, monkeys began dying in the Kyasanur forest in Shivamogga district, Karnataka. Scientists found that ticks there spread a virus, now called Kyasanur Forest Disease.
explanations.art: A tick on a blade of grass with front legs stretched out, and a dog walking past below.

explanations.context: This card is about worms that can live in a person's gut, and how they get in.
explanations.definition: Some worms are parasites who live in the human gut. The commonest in Indian children are roundworms, hookworms and threadworms.
explanations.description: A worm inside the gut has plenty of food. The worm's hard problem is getting from one person to the next. Each kind solves it in their own way. A female roundworm lays thousands of eggs, which leave the body in poo. Where poo gets into soil, the eggs wait there. They get into a new person on dirty hands or unwashed vegetables. Young hookworms wait in damp soil and get in through the skin of bare feet. A threadworm crawls out of the bottom at night to lay eggs, which makes it itch. Scratching puts eggs under the nails, and from there they reach the mouth. So toilets, chappals, washing hands, short nails and washed vegetables close every one of these paths. Twice a year, on National Deworming Day, schools and anganwadis give children a tablet called albendazole that clears worms out.
examples: Wearing chappals on wet soil keeps hookworms out.
Washing hands with soap after the toilet and before eating keeps roundworm and threadworm eggs out of the mouth.
National Deworming Day is on 10 February and 10 August.
explanations.art: A cut-away picture of a child's tummy with a coiled worm inside, and around it a chappal, a bar of soap, a nail cutter and washed vegetables.

explanations.concept: Mosquitoes: why she bites and how she finds you
explanations.context: This card is about mosquitoes: why only females bite, and how they find a person.
explanations.definition: A mosquito is a small fly. Male and female mosquitoes drink nectar and plant juice for energy. Only the female drinks blood, because she needs its protein to make her eggs.
explanations.description: A female mosquito's problem is finding blood in the dark. She follows the carbon dioxide in your breath, the warmth of your body and the smell of your skin and sweat. When she lands, she pushes in her proboscis. Inside its cover are six fine needles. Two saw through the skin, two hold it open, one sucks up blood and one pours in saliva. Her saliva stops your blood from clotting so that it keeps flowing. The itch afterwards is your body reacting to that saliva. If the person she bit before had malaria parasites in their blood, she may now be carrying them. Different mosquitoes bite at different times. Anopheles, who carries malaria, bites mostly from dusk to dawn. Aedes, black with white stripes, bites in the daytime and carries the dengue virus.
examples: Mosquitoes find you more easily after you run and breathe hard, because you breathe out more carbon dioxide.
An Anopheles mosquito rests with her tail end tilted up, at an angle to the wall.
explanations.art: A female mosquito drawn large, with the cover of her proboscis bent back and six fine needles going into skin.

explanations.concept: Malaria: a parasite with two hosts
explanations.context: This card follows the malaria parasite through a mosquito and a person.
explanations.definition: Malaria is an illness caused by Plasmodium, a parasite made of a single cell. The parasite needs two hosts: a person and an Anopheles mosquito.
explanations.description: Here is the journey. A female Anopheles bites a person who has malaria, and drinks parasites with the blood. In the mosquito's stomach the parasites grow and multiply for about one to two weeks. Then they move to her saliva. When she bites someone else, they enter that person's blood. They travel first to the liver and multiply there. Then they move into the red blood cells, multiply again, and burst out. Each time they burst out, the person shivers and then gets a high fever. Malaria can be cured with medicines from a doctor, after a blood test. A medicine called quinine comes from the bark of the cinchona tree. From the 1860s cinchona trees were grown in the Nilgiri hills to make it. In 2024, malaria killed about 610,000 people around the world, most of them young children in Africa.
examples: A fever with shivering, in a place with mosquitoes, is a reason to see a doctor and get a blood test the same day.
A mosquito only carries malaria if she has bitten a person with malaria at least one to two weeks earlier.
explanations.art: A circle of arrows: a mosquito biting a sleeping person, the parasite going to the liver and the blood, and a second mosquito picking the parasite up again.

explanations.context: This card puts together how to keep each parasite off you.
explanations.definition: Every parasite needs a path to reach a new host. Keeping safe means closing that path.
explanations.description: Lice move from head to head, so keep heads apart, check hair with a fine comb each week, and do not share combs or hair clips. Fleas and ticks come from animals and grass, so check pets and wash their bedding, and check your legs after walking in long grass. Worms come from soil and dirty hands, so wear chappals outside, wash hands with soap, keep nails short and wash vegetables. Mosquitoes need water to lay eggs and skin to bite. So cover stored water, empty flowerpot saucers and coolers once a week, sleep under a net, and wear long sleeves at dusk. A fan helps too. Studies have found that fewer mosquitoes reach people sitting in a fan's wind. Mosquitoes are weak fliers, and the wind blows away the breath and smells they follow. If anyone gets a fever with shivering, see a doctor quickly.
examples: A mosquito net over a bed keeps biting mosquitoes out all night.
A lid on a water drum stops mosquitoes from laying eggs in it.
explanations.art: A flat at night with a net over the bed, a fan turning, a lid on a water drum and chappals by the door.

explanations.context: This card asks whether parasites sense the world and make choices.
explanations.description: Parasites sense the world and make choices, like every living being. A tick waits for days on a grass blade and lets go of the grass only when the breath and warmth of an animal come close. A young dodder plant smells the air and grows towards the plant they will feed on. Scientists showed this in 2006: dodder seedlings grew towards the smell of a tomato plant and away from wheat. A female mosquito picks out one person in a room by their smell.
examples: Dodder seedlings grew towards the smell of a tomato plant in a test by Justin Runyon, Mark Mescher and Consuelo De Moraes in 2006.
Some people get many more mosquito bites than others. In tests, mosquitoes chose the smell of their skin again and again.

perspectives.who: Many plant scientists who study how plants behave
perspectives.explanation: Sensing a host, telling one host from another and growing towards them is choosing. A dodder seedling feels and decides where to go.
These are automatic responses to chemicals, built up over millions of years. They work without anything like thought, the way a thermostat switches on a heater.

explanations.art: A thin yellow dodder seedling bending towards a tomato plant and away from a pot of wheat.

agreed.text: Head lice spread mostly by head-to-head contact. They do not jump or fly, and they are not caused by dirty hair.
agreed.evidence: Health services such as the NHS in the United Kingdom say so, from studies of how lice move between children in schools and families.

agreed.text: Malaria is caused by a single-celled parasite, Plasmodium, and is spread by the bite of female Anopheles mosquitoes.
agreed.evidence: Laveran saw the parasite in blood in 1880. Ross found it in mosquitoes in 1897 and 1898, and Grassi's team showed that Anopheles passes it to people in 1898.

agreed.text: Only female mosquitoes drink blood. They need its protein to make eggs.
agreed.evidence: Scientists who raise mosquitoes find that males have mouthparts that cannot pierce skin, and that females lay eggs only after a blood meal.

agreed.text: Hookworms get in through the skin of bare feet, and roundworm eggs are swallowed from soil on hands or food.
agreed.evidence: Doctors have traced these paths for over a hundred years. Where people wear shoes and have toilets, these worms become much rarer.

agreed.text: A tick should be removed with fine tweezers held close to the skin, pulled straight up, slowly and steadily.
agreed.evidence: Health agencies such as the CDC in the United States advise this. Squeezing or burning a tick can leave the mouthparts in the skin.

challenging.claim: Lice come from dirt, so only unwashed children get them.
challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Lice are linked in people's minds with being poor or unwashed, and itching feels dirty.
challenging.against: Lice live on clean hair just as well. Shampoo does not loosen nits. Lice spread when heads touch, which happens to every child.
challenging.context: This card is about a common and hurtful idea: that lice are a sign of a dirty child.

challenging.claim: Malaria comes from bad air rising from swamps at night.
challenging.who: Doctors and ordinary people for more than two thousand years. The name comes from the Italian 'mala aria', bad air.
challenging.for: Malaria was worst near swamps and at night, and people who slept near marshes fell ill.
challenging.against: Swamps and night are when and where Anopheles mosquitoes breed and bite. Ross and Grassi showed in 1897 and 1898 that the parasite travels in mosquitoes. Nets stop malaria, though air passes through them.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that bad air causes malaria.

challenging.claim: Lice can jump from one head to another.
challenging.for: Lice seem to appear on a new head suddenly.
challenging.against: A louse has no wings and no jumping legs. Their claws are made for holding hair, so they crawl across when hairs touch.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that lice jump.

challenging.claim: Some people really are mosquito magnets.
challenging.who: Many people say so, and some scientists have tested it
challenging.for: In tests in 2022, mosquitoes kept choosing the skin smell of certain people, again and again, over months.
challenging.against: How many bites you get also depends on where you sit, your clothes, a fan and how much you breathe out.
challenging.context: This card is about whether mosquitoes like some people more than others.

challenging.claim: Some worms may help the body as well as harm it.
challenging.who: Some doctors and scientists who study the immune system
challenging.for: People and gut worms lived together for a very long time. Some studies suggest that worms calm the body's defences, and that allergies are more common where worms are rare.
challenging.against: Worms cause anaemia and tiredness, and slow children's growth. Other studies found no clear help. Deworming children is still the right thing to do.
challenging.context: This card is about a debated idea: that our bodies may have got used to worms.

big_questions.q: A louse lives on one person's head all their life. Is the louse part of that person, or a separate being?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the louse gets their food and warmth, and what happens if they fall off.

big_questions.q: The malaria parasite cannot finish their life without both a mosquito and a person. Who is the parasite's home?
big_questions.hint: Think of the journey from a person's blood into a mosquito's stomach and back.

big_questions.q: A koel chick is raised by crows. Is the koel mother doing something wrong?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether a crow or a koel follows rules like ours, and what each one needs.

big_questions.q: We kill lice and worms to stay well. Is it fair to kill a living being who is only living their own life?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens to the host if nobody stops the parasites, and about how Jain monks try to harm no living being.

big_questions.q: Your body is home to lice sometimes, and to tiny mites and bacteria all the time. Where do you end and the others begin?
big_questions.hint: Think about your skin, your hair and your gut, and who else lives there.

big_questions.q: Why did a parasite as small as Plasmodium kill more people than tigers, snakes and wars?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many mosquitoes there are, and how easily they reach people.

story.title: Ajji's Comb
story.note: The story is made up. The facts in it are true: nits are glued to the hair close to the scalp and do not wash off, lice spread when heads touch, and they live on clean hair as well as unwashed hair.
text: Kavya was eight, and she lived with her parents and her grandmother in a flat in Mysuru. Her grandmother was called Ajji. Every evening Ajji oiled Kavya's hair with coconut oil and plaited it into one long rope.
One Monday, Kavya came home from school with her head bent low. She dropped her school bag by the door and did not say hello.
"What happened, kanda?" asked Ajji.
Kavya scratched behind her ear. Then she scratched the top of her head. "Divya said I have lice," she whispered. "She said lice are for dirty children. Everyone heard."
Ajji did not laugh, and she did not look shocked. She went to the cupboard and came back with a small comb. It was flat and pale, with teeth so close together that Kavya could hardly see the gaps.
"Come and sit on the step by the window," said Ajji. "We need good light for this."

Kavya sat on the low step with a white towel round her shoulders. Ajji sprinkled water on her hair from a steel tumbler and rubbed in a little oil. Then she parted the hair and began to comb, slowly, from the scalp to the ends.
After each stroke, Ajji wiped the comb on a white tissue. On the fourth stroke there was a tiny brown dot on the tissue. The dot moved.
"There," said Ajji gently. "That is a louse. Look."
Kavya looked. The louse was no bigger than a sesame seed. She had six legs, and she was crawling slowly across the tissue.
"So I am dirty," said Kavya, and her eyes filled with tears.
"Are you?" said Ajji. "You had a head bath on Saturday. I washed your hair myself. Was it dirty?"
Kavya shook her head.

"Then let me show you something." Ajji held up one of Kavya's hairs, close to her eyes. Near the root, almost touching the scalp, there was a tiny pale oval stuck to the hair. "That is a louse egg. We call it a nit. The mother louse glues each egg to a hair, right here, next to your warm scalp. The warmth helps the egg hatch."

Ajji dipped her finger in the tumbler and rubbed the nit with water. It stayed. She rubbed it with a little soap. It still stayed. Only when she pinched the nit between her fingernails and slid it all the way along the hair did it come off.
"You see?" said Ajji. "Soap and water do not move a nit. The glue is too strong. Washing does not keep lice away, and dirt does not bring them. Lice come from other heads."
Kavya thought about that. "But lice cannot jump," she said slowly. "We learned that. They have no wings."
"That's right. So how did they reach your head?"

Kavya remembered. On Friday, the whole class had crowded round Divya's new storybook. They had pressed their heads together to see the pictures. Divya had been in the middle, and Kavya had leaned right against her.
"Our heads touched," said Kavya. "Divya's and mine. And she was scratching all day on Friday."
Ajji nodded. "A louse crawls from one hair to the next when two heads touch. It takes only a moment. It does not matter whether the hair is clean or unwashed."
Kavya sat very still. "Then Divya has lice too. And she said lice are for dirty children."
"Divya probably does not know she has them," said Ajji. "And someone told her that lice mean dirt, the way someone told you. People have said it for a very long time. It is still not true."

Ajji combed for a long time. She combed every part of Kavya's head, front to back and side to side. The tissue collected seven lice and many nits. Then she combed the whole head again, to catch any she had missed.
"Is it finished now?" asked Kavya.

"Not yet. A few eggs always hide. In four days they will hatch, so we will comb again on Friday. Then again, four days after that, and once more after that. By then every louse will be gone before they are old enough to lay eggs."
The next morning, Kavya asked Ajji for two things. The first was the comb, wrapped in a clean handkerchief. The second was a note for Divya's mother.
At school, Kavya found Divya alone by the water tank. Divya was scratching behind her ear.

"I had lice," said Kavya. "I got them from you, I think, when we looked at your book. But it is not because you are dirty. My Ajji showed me. Lice crawl when heads touch. Here, my Ajji wrote how to comb them out."
Divya stared at her. Then she took the note. "I am sorry I said that," she said quietly.
That evening, Kavya told Ajji everything. Ajji smiled and began to oil her hair.
"Ajji," said Kavya, "the louse lives on my head and eats from me, and I never even felt her arrive. Her whole life happens right here." She touched the top of her head. "I am her whole world."
"Yes," said Ajji, "and now you know how to ask her to leave."
story.epiphany: Lice do not come from dirt. A louse crawls across when two heads touch, and her eggs are glued so tightly that washing does not move them. Only a fine comb does.
ask: Why did Ajji rub the nit with water and soap before sliding the nit off with her fingernails?
How did the lice get from Divya's head to Kavya's?
Why did Ajji say they must comb again in four days?
Was Kavya right to take the note to Divya? Why?
art: A grandmother combing a girl's oiled plait on a low step by a window in a Mysuru flat, a white towel round the girl's shoulders.
A white tissue with one tiny brown louse crawling on it, and a fine comb beside it.

games.title: Break the Path: a malaria journey board game
games.context: This is a board game. A malaria parasite tries to travel from a person, into a mosquito and on to a new person. Players play Safety cards to break the path.

printables.title: The journey board
items: A path of 24 squares in a loop.
Squares 1 to 4: in a person's blood.
Square 5: a mosquito bites. Draw a Bite card.
Squares 6 to 12: in the mosquito's stomach. The parasite grows for one to two weeks.
Squares 13 to 15: in the mosquito's saliva.
Square 16: the mosquito bites again. Draw a Bite card.
Squares 17 to 20: in the new person's liver.
Squares 21 to 24: in the new person's red blood cells, then back to square 1.

printables.title: Tokens
items: One parasite token for each player
A die

rules: Each player has a parasite token on square 1.
On your turn, roll the die and move.
On squares 5 and 16, draw a Bite card and do what it says.
The first parasite to go all the way round the loop wins that round. Then ask: which cards helped the parasite, and which broke the path?

flow.do: 1. Cut out the board, the cards and the tokens. 2. Read the squares together.
flow.say: This board is the malaria parasite's journey. Let's read where the parasite goes, from a person's blood to a mosquito and back.
flow.kid: Read the board. Where does the parasite go first? Where next?
flow.context: This is the first step of the malaria journey game. You read the journey before you play.

flow.do: Play one round by the rules.
flow.say: Roll and move. On the bite squares, take a card and do what it says.
flow.kid: Roll the die. Move. On a bite square, take a card.

check.q: In the game, the parasite stays in the mosquito's stomach for many squares. Why?
options: The mosquito is asleep
The parasite must grow there for one to two weeks before they can reach her saliva
The game is slow on purpose
check.why: The parasite grows and multiplies in the mosquito's stomach for about one to two weeks. Only then do they move to her saliva, ready to pass to the next person. If you picked 'the mosquito is asleep', remember that she keeps flying and biting during that time.

flow.do: 1. Sort the cards you drew into 'helped the parasite' and 'broke the path'. 2. Each player writes one new Safety card.
flow.say: Which cards broke the path? Can you invent one more way to stop the journey?
flow.kid: Which cards stopped the parasite? Make up one new card that stops them.

ask.q: Which card do you think breaks the path best, and why?
good: The net, because it stops the bite all night.
Seeing a doctor, because the medicine clears the parasites so no mosquito can pick them up.

setup.caption: 2. On a bite square, draw a Bite card and do what it says.

games.context: This is a sorting card game. Each card shows two living beings who live together. Players decide whether one is a parasite.

printables.title: Score sheet

Cards sorted
Cards where we argued

rules: Lay out the three sorting cards.
Take turns to draw a pair card, read it aloud and place it under one sorting card.
Give a reason each time. Another player may challenge with a different reason.
At the end, check with the answer list. Keep a pile of cards you argued about.

flow.do: 1. Shuffle the pair cards. 2. Take turns to sort them, giving a reason each time.
flow.say: A parasite lives on or in another being and feeds from them. A predator kills and eats. Let's sort each pair, and say why.
flow.kid: Pick a card. Is one of them a parasite? Say why.
flow.context: This is a card game about which living beings are parasites. You sort pairs of beings who live close together.

flow.do: Read the answers and talk about any you disagreed on.
flow.say: Answers: louse, flea, tick, roundworm, hookworm, dodder, koel chick, mosquito and the malaria parasite are parasites. The tiger and the cat are predators. The crow, the bee, curd bacteria, the egret and the mynah are not parasites.
flow.kid: Check the answers. Which ones surprised you?
flow.parent: The mosquito is tricky. She does not live on the person, but she feeds from them and leaves, so many scientists call her a parasite too. The koel is a brood parasite: the mother leaves her eggs for the crows to raise. The mynah helps the cow by eating ticks.

check.q: A koel mother lays her egg in a crow's nest. The crows feed the koel chick. What is the koel chick?
options: A predator
A parasite
A helper of the crows
check.why: The koel chick is fed by the crows, and the crows get nothing back. That makes the koel a parasite of a special kind, a brood parasite. If you picked 'predator', remember a predator kills and eats, and the koel chick does not eat the crows.

setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three sorting cards.

setup.caption: 2. Draw a pair card, say your reason, and place it.

experiments.title: The Comb Test: which comb can catch a louse egg?
experiments.question: A louse egg is smaller than a khus khus seed. Which comb can catch something that small: a wide-tooth comb, an ordinary comb or a fine-tooth lice comb?
experiments.predict: Look at the gaps between the teeth of each comb. Guess which combs will push the sesame seeds along, and which will push the tiny khus khus seeds. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same seeds, the same sheet of paper and the same slow sweep for every comb. Only the comb changes. Do three sweeps with each comb, because one sweep can be a fluke.
results_table: Sesame seeds pushed to the line (out of 10)
Khus khus seeds pushed to the line (out of 10)

materials.item: a fine-tooth lice comb (an eer kolli). Chemists and general stores sell them for about 20 to 50 rupees.
an ordinary hair comb
a wide-tooth comb. No wide comb? Use the wide end of an ordinary comb, if it has one.
10 sesame seeds (ellu or til). Black sesame shows up best on white paper.
10 khus khus seeds (poppy seeds). No khus khus? Use the finest grains of rava.
a sheet of plain paper, a pencil and a ruler
a magnifying glass, if you have one

experiments.safety: Keep the seeds away from babies and small children, who may put them in their nose or mouth. Wash the lice comb before using it on hair.

schedule.what: Look at three combs. Line up sesame and khus khus seeds. Sweep each comb across them three times and count which seeds are pushed along.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the three combs, with the gaps between their teeth, and draw a sesame seed and a khus khus seed to the same size beside them.

setup.art: Three combs lying side by side on a table: a wide-tooth comb, an ordinary comb and a fine-tooth lice comb, with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the three combs side by side and look at the gaps.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a pencil start line and a finish line 10 cm apart, and a row of black sesame seeds and pale khus khus seeds on the start line.
setup.caption: 2. Line up 10 sesame and 10 khus khus seeds on the start line.

setup.art: A child's hand sweeping a comb slowly across the paper, teeth touching it, pushing some seeds along while tiny seeds stay behind between the teeth.
setup.caption: 3. Sweep the comb slowly to the finish line. Count the seeds that reach it.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three combs side by side. 2. Hold each one against the ruler. 3. Count how many teeth fit in 1 cm. 4. Look at the gaps with a magnifying glass if you have one.
flow.say: These three combs have different gaps between their teeth. Let's count how many teeth fit in one centimetre on each comb.
flow.kid: Hold each comb next to the ruler. Count the teeth in 1 cm. Which comb has the smallest gaps?
flow.context: This is the start of the Comb Test. A louse egg is smaller than a khus khus seed. You find out which comb can catch something that small.
flow.parent: A wide-tooth comb may have 2 or 3 teeth in 1 cm. An ordinary comb has about 4 to 8. A lice comb has many more, often 10 or more, with gaps too thin to measure with a school ruler. Counting teeth in 1 cm is a simple way to compare gaps.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess and a reason. 2. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.say: Which comb will push the sesame seeds? Which will push the tiny khus khus seeds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which comb will push the sesame? Which will push the khus khus? Why?

ask.q: What makes you think that comb will catch the small seeds?
good: Its gaps are smaller than the seed.
The seed is too big to slip between its teeth.

flow.parent: Wait for a guess and a reason before going on. Do not explain yet. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Draw a start line across the paper with the pencil. 2. Draw a finish line 10 cm away. 3. Put 10 sesame seeds and 10 khus khus seeds along the start line, mixed up, about 1 cm apart.
flow.say: The seeds are our pretend lice and nits. A sesame seed is about the size of a grown louse. A khus khus seed is a little bigger than a louse egg.
flow.kid: Draw two lines, 10 cm apart. Put the seeds on the first line. Sesame is like a louse. Khus khus is like an egg.

flow.do: 1. Stand the wide-tooth comb on the start line, behind the seeds, with its teeth touching the paper. 2. Sweep it slowly to the finish line. 3. Count the sesame and the khus khus seeds that reached the line. 4. Put them all back and do it twice more.
flow.say: Keep the teeth flat on the paper and move slowly. Then count what reached the finish line.
flow.kid: Put the comb behind the seeds. Teeth touch the paper. Sweep slowly. Count the seeds at the line. Do it three times.
flow.parent: Seeds sometimes jump over the comb or roll sideways. If a seed rolls off the paper, put the seed back and redo that sweep. Pressing the teeth lightly on the paper gives steadier results.

flow.do: Do the same three sweeps with the ordinary comb, and then with the lice comb. Write every count in the table.
flow.say: Now the ordinary comb, three times. Then the lice comb, three times. Same seeds, same lines, same slow sweep.
flow.kid: Now try the ordinary comb three times. Then the lice comb three times. Write each count.
flow.parent: Usually the wide comb pushes some sesame seeds and almost no khus khus, because the small seeds slip between its teeth. An ordinary comb pushes most sesame seeds and some khus khus. The lice comb pushes nearly all of both. Results vary with the comb, so what your child sees is the real result.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask for a claim, the evidence and a reason. 3. Then read out the fact about real nits.
flow.say: Which comb caught the khus khus? What did you see? Why do you think that comb worked? Here is a fact. A real louse egg is smaller than a khus khus seed, and is glued to one hair near the scalp.
flow.kid: Which comb caught the khus khus? Why did it work? A real louse egg is even smaller.

check.q: In the Comb Test, the khus khus seeds slipped past the wide-tooth comb. Why?
options: The seeds were too light
The gaps between the teeth were wider than the seeds
The comb was moved too slowly
check.why: A seed smaller than the gap slips through between two teeth. Only teeth closer together than the seed is wide can push the seed along. That is why only a fine-tooth comb can pull out a louse egg. If you picked 'too light', the sesame seeds were light too, and many of those were pushed.

ask.q: What I think, what I saw, and why?
good: What I think: only a comb with very small gaps catches tiny things. What I saw: the lice comb pushed the khus khus, the wide comb did not. Why: the seeds slipped between the wide teeth.

experiments.title: The Fan Test: where does a fan stop mosquitoes?
experiments.question: Mosquitoes are weak fliers. Where in your bedroom is the fan's wind strong, and where is the air still enough for a mosquito to land?
experiments.predict: Look at the room with the fan on. Guess which places get strong wind and which stay still: the pillow, the foot of the bed, the corners, under the bed. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same paper strip, held at the same height as a sleeping person, with the fan at the same speed. Only the place changes. Hold the strip still for 10 seconds at each place.
results_table: My guess (still, flutters or blows flat)

materials.item: a strip of tissue paper or thin newspaper, about 1 cm wide and 10 cm long
a pencil to tape the strip to, like a small flag
cello tape
a ceiling fan or a table fan
a sheet of paper to draw a map of the room

experiments.safety: A grown-up switches the fan on and off. Never put fingers or the paper near a table fan's blades. Do not stand on a bed or chair under a ceiling fan.

schedule.what: Make a paper flag. Test eight places in the bedroom with the fan on. Draw a wind map, and mark where to put the bed and the pillow.

experiments.record: Draw a map of the room from above. Mark the fan, the bed and each place you tested, with its score. Colour the still places in one colour and the windy places in another.

setup.art: A strip of tissue paper taped to the end of a pencil like a small flag.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a tissue strip to a pencil to make a flag.

setup.art: A child holding the paper flag beside a bed, at the height of the pillow, under a turning ceiling fan, with the strip blowing sideways.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the flag at pillow height in each place for 10 seconds.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a bedroom from above, with numbers 0, 1 and 2 written at different places round the bed.
setup.caption: 3. Score each place and draw a wind map.

flow.do: 1. Tape the tissue strip to the end of the pencil. 2. Choose eight places to test. For example: the pillow, the middle and foot of the bed, each corner and under the bed.
flow.say: This flag shows where the fan's wind reaches. Mosquitoes are weak fliers, so strong wind makes it hard for them to land.
flow.kid: Tape the paper to the pencil. It is a wind flag. Pick eight places to test.
flow.context: This is the start of the Fan Test. A paper flag shows where a fan's wind is strong, and where a mosquito could fly in still air.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason for each place, and write them in the table.
flow.say: Which places will be windy, and which will be still? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess each place. Still, flutters or blows flat? Why?
flow.parent: Wait for the guesses. Many children think the whole room is windy when the fan is on.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up switches the fan on at its usual speed. 2. Hold the flag at the height of a person lying in bed, at each place, for 10 seconds. 3. Score it: 0 still, 1 flutters, 2 blows flat.
flow.say: Hold the flag still and count to ten. Is the paper still, fluttering or blowing flat?
flow.kid: Hold the flag still. Count to ten. Is it still, fluttering or flat? Write the score.
flow.parent: Under a ceiling fan, the wind is usually strongest just below and around the blades, and weaker in the corners and under the bed. A table fan blows mostly in one direction. Results depend on your fan and room, so what you find is the real answer for your room.

flow.do: 1. Draw the wind map. 2. Talk about where the pillow should go.
flow.say: Where are the still places? Mosquitoes can land there easily. Where should the pillow and your face be at night?
flow.kid: Draw your wind map. Where is the air still? Where should your pillow go?

check.q: In the Fan Test, the flag stayed still in a corner. Why might a mosquito find it easier to bite someone sleeping there?
options: Mosquitoes like corners because they are dark
Mosquitoes are weak fliers, and in still air they can fly and land easily
The corner is warmer
check.why: A mosquito flies slowly, so strong wind blows her off course. The wind also blows away the breath and smells she follows. In still air she can find you and land. If you picked 'dark', mosquitoes do rest in dark places, but the wind is what this test showed.

activities.title: How Small? A parasite size line

materials.item: a ruler
a few sesame seeds, khus khus seeds, mustard seeds and grains of rice
one hair
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera zoomed in
a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Keep seeds away from babies and small children.

schedule.what: Match each parasite to a seed of the same size. Draw a size line from the smallest to the biggest.

activities.record: Draw a size line across a page, with each parasite drawn next to the seed or thing of the same size.

setup.art: A ruler on a table with a khus khus seed, a sesame seed, a mustard seed and a grain of rice placed along the ruler.
setup.caption: 1. Put the seeds along a ruler.

setup.art: A notebook page with a line from small to big: a nit, a louse, a flea, a tick, a mosquito, a threadworm and a long roundworm, each drawn beside a seed or a ruler mark.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each parasite beside the seed of the same size.

flow.do: 1. Put a khus khus seed, a sesame seed, a mustard seed and a grain of rice along the ruler. 2. Look at each with the magnifying glass. 3. Lay a hair beside them.
flow.say: These seeds will help us picture how small the parasites are. Which is the smallest? How thick is the hair next to them?
flow.kid: Put the seeds on the ruler. Look with the magnifier. Which is smallest? Look at the hair too.
flow.context: This activity shows how small each parasite is, by matching them to seeds you can hold.

flow.do: Read the sizes aloud and draw each parasite beside the right seed.
flow.say: A louse egg is less than 1 mm long, smaller than a khus khus seed. A louse is up to 3 mm, like a sesame seed. A flea is the same. An unfed tick is a little bigger, and swells to about 1 cm after feeding. A mosquito's body is about as long as a grain of rice. A threadworm is up to about 1 cm. A roundworm can be longer than your ruler.
flow.kid: Draw each one by its seed. Egg by khus khus. Louse by sesame. Mosquito by rice.
flow.parent: These sizes are approximate. A roundworm can grow to about 30 cm or more. The malaria parasite is far too small for this line. They live inside red blood cells, and a red blood cell is less than one hundredth of a millimetre across.

flow.do: Talk about what the line shows.
flow.say: Which parasites could you see on a comb or a tissue? Which one needs a microscope?
flow.kid: Which ones can you see? Which one needs a microscope?

check.q: On your size line, which parasite is far too small to draw?
options: A head louse
The malaria parasite
A tick
check.why: The malaria parasite is a single cell who lives inside a red blood cell. You need a microscope to see them. A louse and a tick are small but easy to see on a white tissue.

activities.title: The Malaria Journey: act it out

materials.item: two chairs or mats as beds, for two 'sleeping people'
a small ball or a ball of paper as the parasite
a dupatta or towel as a mosquito net

activities.safety: Move gently. Keep the play area clear of things to trip on.

schedule.what: Act out the parasite's journey from one person, through a mosquito, to another person. Then act it again with a net.

activities.record: Draw the journey as a circle of arrows, and draw one place where you broke the path.

setup.art: Two children lying on mats, one holding a paper ball, and a third child with arms out like wings buzzing between them.
setup.caption: 1. Two sleepers and one mosquito. The paper ball is the parasite.

setup.art: The same scene with a dupatta draped over one sleeper like a net, and the mosquito stopped outside it.
setup.caption: 2. Act it again with a net, and see where the journey stops.

flow.do: 1. One person lies down holding the paper ball: they have malaria. 2. The mosquito player 'bites' and takes the ball. 3. The mosquito counts slowly to 12, for the days the parasite grows inside her. 4. She 'bites' the second sleeper and hands over the ball.
flow.say: The ball is the malaria parasite. Watch where they go. They live in a person, then in a mosquito, then in a new person.
flow.kid: You are the mosquito. Bite the first sleeper. Take the ball. Count to 12. Bite the next one.
flow.context: This act-out shows the malaria parasite's journey from one person, through a mosquito, to another person.

flow.do: 1. Put the dupatta over the second sleeper as a net. 2. Act it again.
flow.say: Now the second person sleeps under a net. What happens to the parasite's journey?
flow.kid: Now there is a net. Can the mosquito bite? Where does the ball go?

ask.q: Why does the net stop malaria, when air can still pass through it?
good: The net stops the mosquito, and the mosquito carries the parasite.
Malaria is not in the air. It travels inside the mosquito.

flow.do: Talk about other ways to break the journey.
flow.say: Where else could we break the path? Think about the first person, the mosquito and the water she was born in.
flow.kid: Where else can we stop the parasite? Think of three places.
flow.parent: Good answers: the first person sees a doctor and takes medicine, so no mosquito picks up parasites. Covering water means fewer mosquitoes are born. A fan, long sleeves, window mesh or a repellent stop the bite.

activities.title: Weekly Head Check with a Lice Comb

materials.item: a fine-tooth lice comb
a white towel and a white tissue
water in a spray bottle or a tumbler, and conditioner or a little coconut oil
good daylight by a window

activities.safety: A grown-up does the combing gently. Do not use any lice lotion without a grown-up and a chemist's or doctor's advice.

schedule.what: Wet the hair, comb it all with a lice comb over a white towel, and wipe the comb on a tissue after each stroke.

activities.record: Write the date and what you found: nothing, nits, or lice. Do it again on the same day next week.

setup.art: A child sitting by a window with a white towel round the shoulders, while a mother parts the wet hair.
setup.caption: 1. Wet the hair and add conditioner or a little oil.

setup.art: A fine comb being wiped on a white tissue, showing a tiny brown dot.
setup.caption: 2. Comb from the scalp outwards and wipe the comb on a tissue each time.

flow.do: 1. Sit by a window with a white towel round the shoulders. 2. Wet the hair. 3. Rub in conditioner or a little coconut oil.
flow.say: We check everyone's hair once a week, just like brushing teeth. Lice can happen to anyone, so this is nothing to be shy about.
flow.kid: Sit by the window. Towel on your shoulders. Wet hair first.
flow.context: This is a weekly lice check with a fine-tooth comb. Everyone in the family can have one.

flow.do: 1. Part the hair into sections. 2. Comb each section from the scalp to the ends. 3. Wipe the comb on the tissue after every stroke. 4. Look for moving brown dots and for eggs glued near the roots.
flow.say: Tell me if it pulls. Let's see what is on the tissue each time.
flow.kid: Sit still. Look at the tissue after each stroke. See anything move?
flow.parent: Lice are fast and avoid light, so they may be hard to spot. Nits are glued close to the scalp and do not flick off like dandruff. Finding only a few old nits far from the scalp usually means they are empty cases. If you find a living louse, check everyone in the family that day and comb on days 1, 5, 9 and 13.

flow.do: Wash the comb in hot soapy water and write down what you found.
flow.say: We wash the comb so no eggs stay on it. Then we write the date.
flow.kid: Wash the comb. Write today's date and what you found.

check.q: Meena, a girl in Class 3, finds a louse in her hair. What does that tell you?
options: Meena does not wash her hair
Meena's head touched the head of someone who had lice
Meena's cat gave her the louse
check.why: Head lice crawl from head to head when hair touches. They live on clean hair as happily as on unwashed hair, and cats and dogs do not carry human head lice. If you picked 'does not wash', that is a very common idea, and it is wrong.

activities.title: Check the Mosquito Net

materials.item: the family's mosquito net, or a window mesh if you have no net
a ruler
a torch
a needle and thread, or cello tape, to mend holes

activities.safety: A grown-up handles the needle. Do not climb on beds or chairs to reach a net. Ask a grown-up to unhook it.

schedule.what: Count the holes in 1 cm of net. Shine a torch through it to find tears. Mend the tears.

activities.record: Write how many holes fit in 1 cm, how many tears you found and how you mended them.

setup.art: A child holding a ruler against a mosquito net and counting the holes along 1 cm.
setup.caption: 1. Count the holes along 1 cm of net.

setup.art: A torch shining through a white net in a dark room, showing one bigger tear as a bright patch.
setup.caption: 2. Shine a torch through it to find tears.

flow.do: 1. Lay part of the net flat on a table. 2. Hold the ruler on it. 3. Count how many holes fit along 1 cm.
flow.say: A mosquito's body is about as long as a grain of rice. Let's see how small the net's holes are.
flow.kid: Hold the ruler on the net. Count the holes in 1 cm.
flow.context: This activity checks that a mosquito net really keeps mosquitoes out.

flow.do: 1. In a dim room, shine the torch through the net. 2. Look for bright patches where there is a tear. 3. Mend each tear with needle and thread or tape.
flow.say: A mosquito needs only one tear. Let's find every one.
flow.kid: Shine the torch through the net. Look for big bright holes. Those are tears.
flow.parent: Nets most often tear near the bottom, where they are tucked under the mattress, and at the corners. Tucking the net under the mattress all round matters as much as having no tears.

flow.do: Talk about what you found.
flow.say: Why do the holes need to be smaller than a mosquito? Why must the net be tucked in all round?
flow.kid: Why must the holes be small? Why tuck the net in?

check.q: Arjun, a boy in Class 4, sleeps under a net with one tear the size of a coin. Is he safe from mosquitoes?
options: Yes, one small tear does not matter
No, a mosquito can find the tear and come in
Yes, if the fan is off
check.why: A mosquito follows the smell and breath of the sleeper and keeps searching until she finds a way in. A tear the size of a coin is far bigger than she is. Turning the fan off would make it easier for her, not harder.

activities.title: Where Could They Get In? A home detective walk

materials.item: the detective checklist below, copied into a notebook
a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up comes along. Do not touch dirty water or animal bedding with bare hands.

schedule.what: Walk round your home with a checklist. Find each place where a parasite could reach someone, and one fix for each.

activities.record: Fill in the checklist: the place, which parasite could use it, and the fix.

setup.art: A child with a notebook looking into a flowerpot saucer full of water on a balcony.
setup.caption: 1. Look for standing water, where mosquitoes lay eggs.

setup.art: A row of chappals by the door, a shelf with combs, and a dog's bed in a corner, each with a small tick or cross beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Check combs, chappals and pet beds too.

flow.do: Walk round the home and check each item on the list: 1. Flowerpot saucers, buckets, coolers and water drums. 2. Window mesh. 3. Combs and hair clips. 4. Chappals for going out. 5. Soap by every tap. 6. Nail cutter. 7. A pet's bed, if you have a pet.
flow.say: We are parasite detectives. For each place, ask: which parasite could use this, and how do we close the path?
flow.kid: Be a detective. Look at each place on the list. Which parasite could use it?
flow.context: This is a home walk to find every path a parasite could use to reach your family.

flow.do: Choose one fix to do today and one for every week.
flow.say: Which fix can we do right now? Which one should we do every week?
flow.kid: Pick one fix for today. Pick one for every week.
flow.parent: Good fixes: empty and scrub flowerpot saucers and coolers once a week, because mosquito eggs stuck to the sides survive. Cover water drums. Keep one comb for each person. Wear chappals outside.

check.q: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 3, finds water standing in a flowerpot saucer on the balcony. What should she do?
options: Leave it for the plant
Empty it and scrub the saucer, once a week
Add more water
check.why: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water, and the young grow there for about a week. Emptying and scrubbing the saucer each week stops them before they become adults. Scrubbing matters because some mosquito eggs stick to the sides.

activities.title: Pull Out a Pretend Tick

materials.item: a small ball of atta dough
a toothpick broken in half
two raisins
fine tweezers

activities.safety: A grown-up holds the tweezers first and shows how. Tweezers have sharp tips.

schedule.what: Make two pretend ticks in dough. Pull one out the wrong way and one the right way, and compare.

activities.record: Draw the two pulls: the wrong way and the right way, and what was left in the dough each time.

setup.art: A raisin stuck on half a toothpick, pushed into a flat piece of atta dough, like a tick with mouthparts in the skin.
setup.caption: 1. Push a raisin on a toothpick into the dough. That is the tick.

setup.art: Tweezers gripping the toothpick right at the dough's surface, pulling straight up.
setup.caption: 2. Grip right next to the 'skin' and pull straight up, slowly.

flow.do: 1. Flatten the dough. This is the skin. 2. Push a raisin onto each half toothpick. 3. Push both toothpicks deep into the dough.
flow.say: The raisin is the tick's body. The toothpick is their mouthpart, deep in the skin, with barbs like a fish hook.
flow.kid: Flatten the dough. Put a raisin on each toothpick. Push them into the dough.
flow.context: This activity practises the safe way to take a tick off, with a pretend tick in dough.

flow.do: 1. Wrong way: squeeze the first raisin with your fingers and jerk it. 2. Right way: grip the second toothpick with the tweezers right at the dough and pull straight up, slowly.
flow.say: First the wrong way. Squeeze the body and pull fast. Now the right way. Grip close to the skin and pull up slowly.
flow.kid: First squeeze the raisin and pull fast. Then use tweezers close to the dough. Pull slowly.
flow.parent: Squeezing usually pulls the raisin off and leaves the toothpick in the dough, just as squeezing a real tick can leave the mouthparts in the skin. Gripping the toothpick at the surface brings the whole thing out.

flow.do: Compare what is left in the dough.
flow.say: Which way left something behind in the skin? Why does a grown-up grip close to the skin?
flow.kid: Which way left a piece behind? Why grip close to the skin?

check.q: Farhan's dog has a tick. How should a grown-up take the tick off?
options: Pinch the tick's body and pull fast
Grip the tick with fine tweezers right next to the skin and pull straight up, slowly
Burn the tick with a matchstick
check.why: Gripping close to the skin pulls out the mouthparts with the body. Squeezing the body or burning the tick can leave the mouthparts in the skin. Then wash the bite with soap and water.

materials.item: 6 sheets of paper folded and stapled into a booklet
pencils and colours
your size line and notes from this unit

schedule.what: Make the booklet. Write and draw pages for the louse, the flea and the tick.
Write and draw pages for worms, the mosquito and the malaria parasite. Add a 'Close the path' page at the end.

projects.record: The finished booklet, one parasite on each page.

setup.art: A folded paper booklet with 'My Parasite Field Guide' on the cover and a drawing of a louse.

flow.do: 1. Make the booklet. 2. On each page write four headings: Size, Their problem, How their body helps, How to stay safe. 3. Fill in pages for the louse, the flea and the tick.
flow.say: A field guide helps people recognise living beings. For each parasite, first write their problem, then how their body solves it.
flow.kid: Make a booklet. One page for each parasite. Write their problem first.
flow.context: This is the first day of a 2-day project. You make a field guide with one page for each parasite.

check.q: On the louse page, what is the louse's big problem?
options: Finding water
Staying on a head that moves, gets washed and gets combed
Keeping warm at night
check.why: A louse cannot fly or jump, and dies within a day or two off a head. So staying on is everything. Their claws grip single hairs, and the mother glues her eggs near the warm scalp.

challenges.title: Make a Nit Comb
challenges.problem: Make a comb that pushes khus khus seeds along, using only things from home.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
The comb must push at least 8 of 10 khus khus seeds to the finish line in the Comb Test.
It must be safe to hold.
materials: thin sticks from a coconut-leaf broom, or toothpicks
a strip of thick cardboard about 10 cm long
khus khus seeds and the paper from the Comb Test
general: Tape broom sticks side by side along the cardboard, touching each other, so the gaps are smaller than a seed.
Press a strip of cardboard into fine folds, like a fan, and use the folded edge.
creative: Use a toothbrush's bristles as teeth.
Try two rows of teeth, one behind the other, so a seed that slips past the first row is caught by the second.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own comb. Draw it, build it, and test it with the Comb Test. How close must the teeth be?

setup.art: Thin coconut-broom sticks taped side by side along a strip of cardboard, like a comb.
setup.caption: 1. Tape thin sticks close together on cardboard.

setup.art: The homemade comb sweeping across paper, pushing a row of tiny khus khus seeds.
setup.caption: 2. Test it with the Comb Test.

flow.do: Read the problem and draw two ideas.
flow.say: The gaps must be smaller than a khus khus seed. How could we make teeth that close together?
flow.kid: Your comb's gaps must be smaller than a seed. Draw two ideas.
flow.context: This is an engineering challenge. You build a comb that catches seeds as small as a louse egg.

flow.do: Build the comb.
flow.say: Build your best idea. Press the sticks close together.
flow.kid: Build it. Push the teeth close together.
flow.parent: Coconut-broom sticks are thicker at one end. Lay them all the same way and trim them to the same length.

flow.do: 1. Test it with the Comb Test. 2. Improve it and test again. 3. Read the usual and creative ideas.
flow.say: How many khus khus seeds did it push? What could make it better?
flow.kid: Test it. How many seeds reached the line? Make it better.

challenges.title: Cover the Water
challenges.problem: A family stores water in an open bucket on the balcony. Design a cover so no mosquito can lay eggs on the water, while the family can still take water out easily.
constraints: No gap bigger than a grain of rice.
The water must be easy to take out.
materials: an old cotton cloth or an old piece of mosquito net
general: Stretch a cloth over the top and tie it tight with string all round the rim.
Use a tight-fitting lid, and keep it on all the time.
creative: Cut a small flap in the cloth for a mug, with a second cloth hanging over it.
Put a tap low on the side of a drum, so the lid never needs to come off.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own cover. Draw it, make it, and test it with a grain of rice: can the rice get through anywhere?

flow.kid: Mosquitoes lay eggs on water. How can you cover it? Draw two ideas.
flow.context: This is a design challenge. You make a cover that keeps mosquitoes off stored water.

flow.do: Make the cover and test it with a grain of rice at the edges.

flow.kid: Make your cover. Can a grain of rice get in at the edge?
flow.parent: A grown-up carries the full bucket. A cloth tied tight with string all round the rim usually leaves no gap.
