opts: A living being who kills and eats another
A living being who lives on or inside another living being and feeds from them
quiz.why: A parasite lives on or in a host and takes food from them. A being who kills and eats another is a predator. Many small beings, such as ants, are not parasites.

quiz.p: A dog has fleas. What do we call the dog?
quiz.why: The host is the living being a parasite lives on. A vector carries a parasite from one host to another, as a mosquito carries malaria.

quiz.p: In the Comb Test, which comb pushed the tiny khus khus seeds to the line?
quiz.why: Only the lice comb's gaps were narrower than the seeds. The small seeds slipped between the teeth of the wider combs. A real louse egg is smaller than a khus khus seed, so only a fine comb lifts the egg out.

quiz.p: How do head lice get from one child to another?
opts: They crawl across when two heads touch
quiz.why: Lice have no wings and cannot jump. Their claws are made for gripping hair, so they crawl from hair to hair when heads touch.

quiz.p: Why do shampoo and water not remove nits?
opts: Nits are hidden inside the hair
The mother louse glues each egg firmly to a hair
Nits are too heavy to wash away
quiz.why: The glue is very strong and water does not loosen it. A fine comb, or sliding the nit off with fingernails, is needed.

quiz.p: A tick waits on a blade of grass. How does the tick know an animal is coming?
opts: The tick hears the animal's footsteps
The tick's front legs sense the animal's breath, warmth and smell
The tick sees the animal from far away
quiz.why: Ticks hold out their front legs, which have sense organs for carbon dioxide, warmth and smell. When an animal brushes past, the tick grabs on.

quiz.p: How does a flea get on to a big animal like a dog?
opts: The flea jumps, using a springy pad in their legs
The flea waits to be licked up
quiz.why: Fleas have no wings. A pad of springy resilin in their legs works like a catapult, so a flea can jump about a hundred times their own length.

quiz.p: Kavya walks barefoot on wet soil in a village. Which worm could get in through her feet?
quiz.why: Young hookworms live in damp soil and get in through the skin of bare feet. Roundworm and threadworm eggs are swallowed from dirty hands or food. Chappals keep hookworms out.

quiz.p: Which habit stops roundworm eggs from reaching your mouth?
opts: Washing hands with soap before eating, and washing vegetables
quiz.why: Roundworm eggs come from soil, on hands and on vegetables. Washing removes them. A net stops mosquitoes, not worm eggs.

quiz.p: Why does only the female mosquito drink blood?
opts: She needs protein from blood to make her eggs
She is bigger than the male
quiz.why: Both males and females drink nectar for energy. The female also needs the protein in blood to make her eggs.

opts: A tiny one-celled parasite carried by Anopheles mosquitoes
quiz.why: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a single-celled parasite. Female Anopheles mosquitoes carry the parasite from person to person. People once blamed bad air, and the name malaria means bad air in Italian.

quiz.p: In 1897, in Secunderabad, what did Ronald Ross find?
opts: Malaria parasites growing in the stomach of a mosquito
quiz.why: Ross let mosquitoes feed on a person with malaria, then cut them open and found the parasites growing in a mosquito's stomach. That showed mosquitoes carry malaria.

items.p: Which of these is a parasite?
items.why: A head louse lives on a person's head and drinks their blood. A bee helps flowers, and a tiger is a predator who kills and eats.
items.art: A bee, a louse and a tiger in a row.

items.p: The living being a parasite lives on or in is called the ____.
items.why: The host gives the parasite a home and food.

items.p: Head lice can jump from one head to another.
items.why: False. Lice have no jumping legs and no wings. They crawl from hair to hair when heads touch.

items.p: Lice live on clean hair as well as on unwashed hair.
items.why: True. Lice need warmth and blood, not dirt. Getting lice says nothing about how clean someone is.

items.p: A louse's egg is called a ____.
items.why: A nit is a louse egg glued to a hair near the scalp, or the empty case left after hatching.

items.p: In the Comb Test, why did the khus khus seeds slip past the wide-tooth comb?
opts: The gaps were wider than the seeds
items.why: A seed smaller than the gap slips between two teeth. Only teeth closer together than the seed can push the seed along.

items.p: Sort these parasites. Do they live on the outside of the body or inside it?
items: head louse
Outside
roundworm
Inside
tick
Outside
hookworm
Inside
flea
Outside
malaria parasite
Inside
items.why: Lice, ticks and fleas hold on to hair or skin. Worms live in the gut, and the malaria parasite lives in the liver and blood.

items.p: How many legs does an adult tick have?
items.why: Ticks are arachnids, cousins of spiders, and adults have eight legs. Insects such as lice and fleas have six.

items.p: Only female mosquitoes bite.
items.why: True. Females need protein from blood to make eggs. Males drink only nectar and plant juice.

items.p: Which of these keeps mosquitoes from laying eggs at home?
opts: Emptying and scrubbing saucers and coolers once a week
items.why: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water, and the young take about a week to grow. Emptying the water each week stops them.

items.p: Match each parasite to how they reach a person.
pairs: eggs are swallowed from dirty hands
items.why: Each parasite has one main path. Closing that path keeps them out.

items.p: Put the malaria parasite's journey in order.
items: The parasites move to the mosquito's saliva
A mosquito bites a person with malaria
The mosquito bites a new person
The parasites grow in the mosquito's stomach
a: A mosquito bites a person with malaria
The parasites grow in the mosquito's stomach
The parasites move to the mosquito's saliva
The mosquito bites a new person
items.why: The parasite needs a person and a mosquito. They grow in the mosquito for one to two weeks before they can pass on.

items.p: Kavya and her friend Divya both have head lice. Three grown-ups each say what to do.

views.says: Cut the hair very short. Then there is nothing for lice to hold.
Comb wet hair with a fine lice comb on days 1, 5, 9 and 13.
Use a lice lotion, following the instructions exactly, and comb afterwards.

items.ask: Which would you choose? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one good point about another choice.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason from the science. For example, combing four times, four days apart, catches the lice that hatch from eggs the comb missed. It then names a fair good point of another choice, such as a lotion killing lice in one go, or short hair being quick to comb.
items.why: All three can work, and each has a cost. Combing takes time but uses no chemicals. A lotion needs a grown-up and care. Cutting hair short is quick but many children do not want it.

items.p: Why does a mosquito net stop malaria, even though air passes through it?
items.a: Malaria is not in the air. The parasite is carried by a mosquito. The net's holes are smaller than a mosquito, so she cannot reach you to bite.
items.why: A full answer says that the mosquito carries the parasite and the net keeps the mosquito out.

items.p: Draw a head louse holding a hair, with an egg glued near the scalp.
items.a: A small insect with six legs, each ending in a claw round the hair, and a small oval egg on the hair close to the scalp.
items.why: Claws let the louse stay on. The egg is glued near the scalp because warmth helps the egg hatch.
items.art: An outline of a few hairs growing from a scalp.

items.p: A louse falls off a child's head onto a cushion. What usually happens to the louse?
opts: She lives on the cushion for months
She dies within a day or two
items.why: A head louse needs blood and warmth from a head. Away from one, she usually dies within a day or two. That is why there is no need for big cleaning of the house.

items.p: A mother louse glues each egg to a hair right next to the scalp. Why there, and not at the end of the hair?
items.a: The scalp is warm, and the eggs need warmth to hatch. At the end of the hair it is cooler, and the egg could be cut off or combed out more easily.
items.why: A strong answer names the louse's problem, keeping the eggs warm and safe, and says how gluing them near the scalp solves it.

items.p: A fine comb must be used on days 1, 5, 9 and 13, because one combing can miss eggs.
items.why: True. Eggs hatch in about 8 days. Combing every four days catches young lice before they are old enough to lay eggs.

items.p: A flea's body is flat from side to side. How does that help the flea?
opts: The flea can slide between an animal's hairs
items.why: A thin, flat body slips between hairs. Backward-pointing spines also make the flea hard to pull out.

items.p: Why should a grown-up never squeeze a tick's body to pull the tick off?
opts: The tick will bite the grown-up
Squeezing can leave the barbed mouthparts in the skin
items.why: A tick's mouthpart has backward barbs and is often glued in. Squeezing pulls the body off and leaves the mouthpart behind. Grip close to the skin with fine tweezers and pull straight up.

items.p: Sort these. Which parasite does each habit stop?
items: one comb for each person
Lice
chappals outside
Worms
a net over the bed
Mosquitoes
washing hands before eating
Worms
a weekly check with a fine comb
Lice
covering water drums
Mosquitoes
items.why: Each habit closes the path one parasite uses.

items.p: A threadworm makes a child's bottom itch at night. How do threadworm eggs get back into the mouth?
opts: Scratching puts eggs under the nails, and from there they reach the mouth
items.why: The female lays eggs around the bottom at night. Scratching picks them up on fingers. So short nails and washing hands in the morning help.

items.p: A mosquito bites a person with malaria today. When could she first pass malaria on?
opts: After about one to two weeks
items.why: The parasites must grow in her stomach and move to her saliva first. That takes about one to two weeks.

items.p: Mosquitoes find people by the carbon dioxide they breathe out, their warmth and their smell.
items.why: True. That is why the wind from a fan, which blows these away, means fewer mosquitoes find you.

items.p: In the Fan Test, the paper flag stayed still under the bed. What does this tell you?
opts: The air there is still, so a mosquito can fly and rest there easily
items.why: Mosquitoes are weak fliers. Still places are where they can fly and rest easily.

items.p: The malaria parasite's name is ____.
items.why: Plasmodium is a single-celled parasite who lives in people and in Anopheles mosquitoes.

items.p: Match each mosquito to what she carries.
items.why: Anopheles bites mostly from dusk to dawn. Aedes bites in the daytime and breeds in clean stored water.

items.p: Divya says, 'Lice are for dirty children.' What would you tell her? Give one reason.
items.a: Lice live on clean hair too. They crawl across when heads touch, and washing does not remove their eggs. So anyone can get lice.
items.why: A good answer gives a reason from the science: how lice spread, or that washing does not move nits.

items.p: Dodder is a yellow plant with no green leaves. Dodder winds round another plant and takes food from their ____.
items.why: Dodder pushes tiny suckers into the host plant's stem and takes food from inside it.

items.p: Draw the malaria journey as a circle with four arrows: person, mosquito stomach, mosquito saliva, new person.
items.a: A circle of four labelled stages joined by arrows, in that order.
items.why: The parasite needs both hosts, in this order.
items.art: An empty circle with four boxes on it.

items.p: In the Comb Test, Meenakshi's wide comb pushed 9 of 10 sesame seeds but only 1 of 10 khus khus seeds. What is the best explanation?
opts: The sesame seeds were bigger than the gaps, and most khus khus seeds were smaller
She swept faster for the khus khus
items.why: Seeds bigger than the gap get pushed. Seeds smaller than the gap slip through. The one khus khus seed pushed may have been stuck against a sesame seed or a tooth.

items.p: A louse egg hatches in about 8 days. The young louse becomes an adult who can lay eggs about 9 days later. If you comb only once, what could happen?
opts: Eggs the comb missed hatch, grow up and lay new eggs
Nothing, because one combing gets every egg
The lice leave on their own
items.why: One combing always misses a few eggs. Combing every four days catches the young lice before they are old enough to lay eggs.

items.p: Why is it hard for a parasite inside the gut to reach a new host?
opts: They must leave the body, survive outside, and get into someone else
items.why: Inside the gut there is plenty of food. The hard part is the journey to a new person, through soil, hands, food or skin.

items.p: A mosquito net stops malaria because air cannot pass through it.
items.why: False. Air passes through a net easily. The net stops the mosquito, and the mosquito is what carries the parasite.

items.p: People once thought malaria came from bad air near swamps at night. Why did the idea seem right?
opts: Swamps and night are where and when Anopheles mosquitoes breed and bite
People never got malaria in the daytime
items.why: The bad air idea matched what people saw, but the real cause was the mosquitoes who breed in still water and bite at night.

items.p: A tick has no wings and cannot jump. Explain how a tick still finds a host.
items.a: The tick climbs a grass blade and holds out their front legs. The legs sense the breath, warmth and smell of an animal coming close. When the animal brushes past, the tick grabs on.
items.why: A full answer says the tick waits, senses the animal and grabs on.

items.p: Farhan's family empties their cooler once a month. Mosquitoes take about a week to grow from egg to adult in water. Is once a month enough? Explain.
items.a: No. In a month, about four batches of mosquitoes could grow up and fly away. The cooler must be emptied and scrubbed at least once a week, so no young mosquitoes have time to become adults.
items.why: A strong answer compares the two times, a week to grow and a month between emptying, and says what follows.

items.p: A koel mother lays her egg in a crow's nest, and the crows raise the koel chick. Three voices talk about it.

views.says: She tricked us. We fed her chick instead of our own.
This is how koels have always raised chicks. We never build nests of our own.
Crows and koels have shaped each other for a very long time. Crows chase koels away, and koels lay their eggs quickly when the crows are away.

items.ask: Which voice do you agree with most? Use what you learned about parasites and hosts. Then answer back from another voice.
items.a: A strong answer picks a voice and backs it with facts from the unit: what a host gives, what a parasite takes, and how each has changed the other. Then it answers back fairly from a second voice.
items.why: There is no single right answer. The crow loses food and work, the koel has no other way to raise chicks, and the scientist describes how both have changed over time.

items.p: Most parasites kill their host quickly.
items.why: False. Most parasites harm their host a little and live with them for a long time. A host who dies quickly takes the parasite's home and food away.

items.p: The malaria parasite needs two hosts. Name them, and say what happens in each.
items.a: A person and an Anopheles mosquito. In the person, the parasites grow in the liver and then in red blood cells, causing fever. In the mosquito, they grow in the stomach and move to the saliva, ready to pass on.
items.why: A full answer names both hosts and one thing that happens in each.

items.p: Kavya has a fever with shivering, and there are many mosquitoes where she lives. What should her family do?
opts: Wait a week to see if it goes
Take her to a doctor for a blood test the same day
items.why: Malaria can be cured, but it is dangerous if left. A blood test shows the parasite, and the right medicine clears them.

items.p: Ross found malaria parasites in a mosquito's stomach in 1897. Why was that not yet proof that mosquitoes give malaria to people?
opts: He also needed to show that a mosquito's bite passes the parasite to a new host
items.why: Finding the parasite in a mosquito showed she could pick the parasite up. In 1898 Ross showed bites passing malaria between birds, and Grassi's team showed Anopheles passing it to people.

items.p: Sort these. Which are parasites and which are predators?
items: flea on a cat
Parasite
cat catching a mouse
Predator
tick on a cow
Parasite
spider eating a fly
Predator
roundworm in a person
Parasite
owl catching a rat
Predator
items.why: A parasite feeds from a living host and usually keeps them alive. A predator kills and eats their prey.

items.p: Choose one parasite. Write their problem, then how their body solves it.
items.a: For example: a louse must stay on a moving head. Their claws grip single hairs, and the mother glues her eggs near the warm scalp.
items.why: A good answer starts with the parasite's own problem and then names the body part that helps.

items.p: Design a sign for your building's notice board that tells neighbours how to stop mosquitoes breeding. Use pictures and at most 10 words.
items.a: For example: a bucket with a lid, an empty flowerpot saucer and the words 'Empty and cover water every Sunday'.
items.why: A good sign shows a real fix clearly, in very few words.
items.art: A blank notice with a border.

Mosquito nets, window mesh and covered water tanks protect homes from malaria and dengue.
National Deworming Day gives worm medicine to children in schools and anganwadis twice a year.
Health workers test a drop of blood for malaria parasites under a microscope, or with a quick test kit.
City health teams check homes and building sites for still water where mosquitoes breed.
Vets check dogs and cats for fleas and ticks.
Doctors use what is known about each parasite's path to decide how to stop an outbreak.
Scientists study louse DNA to learn when people first began to wear clothes.

open_questions.q: Can malaria ever be wiped out completely?
open_questions.why_open: Many countries, including Sri Lanka in 2016, have ended malaria. But mosquitoes are learning to survive insecticides and parasites to survive medicines, so nobody knows whether the whole world can.

open_questions.q: Why do some people get many more mosquito bites than others?
open_questions.why_open: Tests show that skin smell matters a lot, but scientists do not yet fully know which smells, or why they differ from person to person.

open_questions.q: Do gut worms help the body in any way?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies suggest worms calm the body's defences and lower allergies. Others find no clear help. The question is still argued about.

open_questions.q: What is it like to be a tick, waiting for weeks on a blade of grass?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure what a tick senses, but nobody knows what that waiting is like from the inside.

open_questions.q: Exactly how many kinds of parasites are there?
open_questions.why_open: Many parasites are tiny and live inside other animals, so most have never been counted or named. Some scientists think there may be more parasite species than free-living ones.

maths.problem: A louse egg hatches about 8 days after being laid. The young louse becomes an adult about 9 days after hatching. How many days is it from egg to adult?
maths.explain: 8 days as an egg, then 9 days growing. 8 + 9 = 17. So a family that combs every 4 days, on days 1, 5, 9 and 13, catches every young louse long before day 17, when they could start laying eggs.
maths.context: This is about how fast head lice grow, and why families comb again and again.
maths.why_maths: Adding the days shows why combing four times, four days apart, is enough to stop the lice.

maths.problem: A female louse can lay up to 6 eggs a day. What is the most eggs she could lay in one week?
maths.explain: A week is 7 days. 7 lots of 6 is 42. So one louse missed by the comb can quickly mean many more, which is why every part of the head is combed.
maths.context: This is about how many eggs one louse can lay.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how fast one louse can become many, and why a careful comb-through matters.

maths.problem: In the Comb Test, Meenakshi pushed the khus khus seeds three times with each comb. Out of 10, the wide comb pushed 1, 0 and 2. The ordinary comb pushed 4, 6 and 5. The lice comb pushed 10, 9 and 10. Which comb would you use to remove nits, and how sure are you?
maths.answer: The lice comb. Every sweep it pushed 9 or 10 seeds, while the others never pushed more than 6.
maths.explain: Add each comb's sweeps. Wide: 1 + 0 + 2 = 3 out of 30. Ordinary: 4 + 6 + 5 = 15 out of 30. Lice comb: 10 + 9 + 10 = 29 out of 30. The lice comb's worst sweep, 9, beats the ordinary comb's best sweep, 6. So we can be sure the result is not a fluke.
maths.context: Remember the Comb Test, where you swept three combs across sesame and khus khus seeds? Here are some made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the best and worst sweeps tells us whether one comb is really better, or whether we were lucky.

maths.problem: On 3 August, a mosquito bites a person with malaria. The parasites need about 12 days in her body before she can pass them on. On which date could she first pass on malaria?
maths.explain: 3 + 12 = 15, so 15 August. This shows something surprising. A young mosquito cannot pass on malaria. Only a mosquito who lives more than about 12 days after biting a sick person can. That is why stopping mosquitoes from living long, with nets and covered water, works so well.
maths.context: This is about how long the malaria parasite takes to grow inside a mosquito.
maths.why_maths: Counting on through the calendar shows that only older mosquitoes can carry malaria.

maths.problem: A cat flea is about 2 mm long and can jump about 20 cm. How many times their own length is that? If a child 120 cm tall could jump the same number of times their height, how far would that be?
maths.answer: About 100 times. The child would jump about 12,000 cm, which is 120 metres.
maths.explain: 20 cm is 200 mm. 200 divided by 2 is 100. Then 120 cm times 100 is 12,000 cm. 100 cm make 1 metre, so that is 120 metres, longer than a cricket ground.
maths.context: This is about how far a flea can jump compared with their size.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a jump with the jumper's own size shows how special the flea's spring really is.

roots.context: We have met lice, fleas, ticks, worms and the malaria parasite, and tested which comb catches a louse egg. Now we ask what parasites tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Comb Test, most khus khus seeds slipped between the teeth of the wider combs. A louse egg is smaller still, and glued to one hair near the warm scalp. A head louse lives only on people, and dies within a day or two off a head. So a louse's home is a living person, who moves, washes and combs.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a home as a place, like a house, a nest or a pond. For a parasite, the home is another living being. That home breathes, grows, scratches and fights back, and a parasite's whole body is shaped to stay in it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Comb Test, only the fine-tooth lice comb pushed the khus khus seeds along. A real nit is smaller than a khus khus seed and glued to the hair, so a louse family survives everything a head does except a very fine comb. Away from a head, a louse dies within a day or two.

three.who_am_i: You are a host. Lice can live in your hair, and tiny mites live in the skin of nearly every grown-up's face.
three.what_is_life: The malaria parasite cannot finish their life in one body. They need a person and a mosquito, one after the other.
three.what_is_this_world: All over the world, living beings live on and inside other living beings: dodder on plants, koel chicks in crows' nests, worms in guts.

roots.thread: A louse, a flea, a tick, a worm and the malaria parasite are very different beings. Yet each one lives on the life of another. The blood that keeps you alive also feeds the louse in your hair and the mosquito at your window. One life, yours, holds up several others at the same time. A host and a parasite have lived together for so long that each one's body has been shaped by the other.

teachings.teaching: All breathing, living beings should not be killed, harmed or treated with violence. This is the pure and lasting law.
teachings.link: Jain monks take great care not to harm even tiny beings. A louse is a living being with their own life, and the Jain teaching asks us to notice that, even while we comb lice out to keep ourselves well. Combing gently with a fine comb removes lice without poisons.

teachings.teaching: Find the illness, then find its cause, then find what will end it, and then act.
teachings.link: This is how malaria was solved. Laveran found the parasite, Ross found the mosquito that carries them, and now we act by closing that path with nets, covered water and medicine.

science.text: Human head lice and chimpanzee lice split into separate kinds about 5 to 6 million years ago, around the time people and chimpanzees did. Lice have lived on our ancestors all that time.
Body lice, who live in clothes, split from head lice when people began wearing clothes, perhaps between about 83,000 and 170,000 years ago.
What a louse or a tick senses and feels from the inside is not known.

other_view.view: A parasite is simply a living being who uses another for food, and the right response is to remove them. Thinking about a louse's home or a louse's life can make people slow to treat lice, worms and malaria, which harm children. Health comes first.

practice.title: Feel the warmth they need
practice.say: Let's sit still and close our eyes. Put both hands gently on top of your head. Feel how warm your scalp is. That warmth is what a louse egg needs to hatch. Now put your hands on your tummy and feel it rise and fall. Your breath is what a mosquito follows. Take five slow breaths. Your warmth and your breath reach out into the world, and other living beings notice them.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Put your hands on your head. Feel the warmth. Now hands on your tummy. Breathe slowly five times. Others can sense your warmth and breath.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the materials listed. Choices made: no real lice, worms or mosquitoes are handled. The Comb Test uses sesame seeds as lice and khus khus as nits, swept across paper, because seeds sprinkled into hair or thread fall out and give no countable result. Black sesame shows best on white paper, and fine rava can replace khus khus. Results vary with the combs, so the steps describe the usual pattern and say that the child's own result is the real one. Teeth per centimetre is used to compare gaps, because a lice comb's gaps are too thin for a school ruler. The Fan Test uses a tissue flag at pillow height, never near a table fan's blades. The tick activity uses a raisin on a toothpick in atta dough: squeezing pulls the raisin off and leaves the toothpick, just as squeezing a real tick leaves the mouthparts. The net check uses a torch in a dim room to find tears. The head check is done by a grown-up, and no lice lotion is suggested without a chemist or doctor. Mosquito larvae are not studied here, because the life cycles unit already has a wriggler check. The spine is the intro, the size line, the Comb Test, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: For more than two thousand years, people blamed malaria on bad air. The name comes from the Italian 'mala aria', which means bad air. People thought foul air rising from swamps at night made them ill. In 1880, Alphonse Laveran, a French army doctor in Algeria, looked at a sick soldier's blood under a microscope. He saw tiny moving living beings inside it: the malaria parasite. But how did the parasite get from one person to another? Patrick Manson, a British doctor, had found that mosquitoes carry tiny worms from person to person. He guessed they might carry malaria too. Ronald Ross, a doctor born in Almora, tested the idea in India. For two years he let mosquitoes feed on people with malaria, then cut the mosquitoes open and searched. On 20 August 1897, in Secunderabad, next to Hyderabad, he found the parasites growing in the stomach of a mosquito with spotted wings, an Anopheles. In 1898 in Calcutta, with his helper Muhammad Bux, he showed that mosquito bites passed malaria between birds. That year, Giovanni Battista Grassi's team in Italy showed that Anopheles mosquitoes pass malaria to people. The bad air idea was wrong.
how_we_found_out.who: Alphonse Laveran, Patrick Manson, Ronald Ross with Muhammad Bux, and Giovanni Battista Grassi
how_we_found_out.when: 1880 (Laveran sees the parasite) to 1897 and 1898 (Ross and Grassi find the mosquito path)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought malaria came from bad air rising from swamps at night. Ross and Grassi showed that a parasite causes it, and a female Anopheles mosquito carries the parasite from one person to the next. Swamps and night mattered only because that is where and when these mosquitoes breed and bite.
